skill.name: Find it: locate the exact detail that answers a question
skill.why: The answer is usually sitting in the text. Finding the exact words proves it.
skill.how: Spot the question's key word, find it in the text, then read around it.

It was a brushtail possum, and it had a string of tinsel wrapped around its tail. The next morning, Dad found the hole in the roof where it had squeezed in. encounters.frame: A waterproof logbook has washed up on Hollowgum's beach. The Squintle won't stop staring at it.
encounters.text: Research ship Southern Petrel, Day 4. At 0600 we lowered the submersible, which the crew calls the Tin Can, into the trench off Cape Brindle. Dr Okafor piloted, and I sat beside her with the cameras, trying not to think about the two kilometres of water waiting below us. The Tin Can is about the size of a family car, and it smells of cold coffee and nervous people. At 800 metres the last trace of sunlight vanished, and the only light came from tiny glowing creatures drifting past like sparks. At 1,400 metres we spotted our first target: a ghost shark, pale and silvery, with eyes like dinner plates. It circled us twice before disappearing into the gloom. The real surprise came at 1,900 metres, where the sea floor was carpeted with thousands of purple sea cucumbers, all slowly vacuuming the mud. Some were as long as my arm. Dr Okafor laughed so hard she fogged up the window. We collected three samples with the robotic arm, although one sea cucumber defended itself by squirting its sticky insides all over the claw. We began our ascent at 1130 and surfaced at 1340, starving and slightly seasick. Tomorrow we dive again, this time hoping to find the giant sea louse that was filmed here in 1998.
encounters.prompt: How long was the Tin Can underwater, from going in to coming back up?

encounters.text: REVIEW: LANTERN DRIFT, by Zed. Lantern Drift is a puzzle game in which you guide a paper lantern down a river at night, lighting up hidden paths for a lost fox cub. Each level adds something new, such as whirlpools, sleeping owls or floating ice. There are forty levels, and each one takes about five minutes, although the final level took me nearly an hour and two packets of crackers. The controls are simple: tilt the screen to steer, and tap to make the lantern glow brighter. Glowing brighter uses up oil, so you have to decide when the extra light is worth it. The fox cub follows close behind and gives a tiny yip whenever it finds a star. The music is gentle and plinky, which I liked at first but found slightly annoying by level thirty. The best feature is the photo mode, which lets you pause anywhere and snap the scenery, and I have taken about three hundred shots of the same waterfall. My only real complaint is that you can't replay a level once you have finished it, so if you miss a hidden star, it's gone for good. Overall, Lantern Drift is calm, clever and occasionally frustrating. I give it eight lanterns out of ten.

encounters.frame: Wren is reading a letter from the wildlife park to the class. She has written four plans for the visit.
encounters.text: Dear Year 5/6 at Hollowgum Primary, thank you for raising $340 to adopt Dot, our southern cassowary, for the year. Your money will pay for her fruit, which is a big job, because Dot eats about five kilograms of it a day and is extremely fussy about her figs. You asked lots of questions in your letter, so here are some answers. Dot turns twenty-two on Monday the 7th of May, and she is already the oldest bird in the park. She has a bony helmet on her head called a casque, and nobody is quite sure what it is for. She weighs fifty-eight kilograms, about the same as a grown-up, and she can run at nearly fifty kilometres an hour, which is why her keepers never turn their backs on her. The bright blue skin on her neck goes even brighter when she is cross, which is usually at the leaf blower. Her keepers say she is clever, moody and very good at stealing hats. As her adopters, you are invited to a behind-the-scenes visit two days after her birthday. The main gate does not open until ten, so please be at the side gate at least half an hour before that. Wear closed shoes, and please do not bring any fruit, or Dot will follow you home. Yours sincerely, Lena Ward, Head Keeper

encounters.frame: Tully retold the cross-country report in her own words for the Reef Rays newsletter. One detail is wrong.
encounters.text: CROSS-COUNTRY CHAOS AT HOLLOWGUM. This year's inter-school cross-country was run in conditions that one teacher described as 'like jogging through warm porridge'. Overnight rain had turned the three-kilometre course into a mud bath, and organisers delayed the start by forty-five minutes while volunteers laid straw over the worst patches. The course wound through the paddocks behind the school and crossed Gum Creek twice. When the Year 6 boys' race finally began at 10.15, the early leader, Kai Ferris, lost a shoe in the first hundred metres and ran the rest of the course in one sock. Despite this, he finished second, just three seconds behind Ollie Brand from Pine Gully Primary. The girls' race was won by Hollowgum's own Tia Mahoney, who led from start to finish and crossed the line in eleven minutes and forty seconds, almost a minute clear of the next runner. Hollowgum finished third overall, behind Pine Gully and Seabreeze, and will host the event again next year. Officials later found more than sixty shoes stuck in the mud near the creek crossing. They are being kept in the school hall, and families have been asked to collect them by the end of the week, preferably while wearing a peg on their nose.

encounters.frame: Mo is telling everyone how he caught a ghost. Check the real order of events.
encounters.text: By the time the police car pulled up outside the old Gully Road post office, the 'ghost' had already been caught, and it was sitting on the front step eating a sausage roll. The whole thing had begun three nights earlier, when Mrs Petrakis, who lives across the road, saw a pale shape drifting past the post office windows at two in the morning. She rang her nephew, who posted about it online, and by the next evening a crowd of ghost hunters had gathered on the footpath with torches and phones. Nothing happened that night, apart from a great deal of shivering. On the second night, someone heard a low moaning sound, and two teenagers ran off so fast that they left a scooter behind. It was Mo, of all people, who solved it. On the third night, while everyone else was staring at the windows, he noticed fresh footprints in the dust leading round the back. He followed them to a broken window and found a skinny backpacker named Felix. Felix had been sleeping inside the empty building, wrapped in a white sheet to keep warm, and moaning because the floorboards were so uncomfortable. He now has a bed at the youth hostel, and Mrs Petrakis brings him lamingtons.
